subtopic: WILDLIFE
WILDLIFE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's extensive forests are the home of a rich and varied wildlife. Unfortunately, all too often harvesting the forests destroys the habitat upon which wildlife depends.
This does not have to be. An effort must be made to integrate wildlife and forestry management policies and practices. Therefore we urge the Government to incorporate wildlife conservation goals in federal and provincial forestry agreements when they are renegotiated this fall.
On April 14 a full day on Parliament Hill will be devoted to wildlife. On that day parliamentarians will have an opportunity to hear organizations and groups speak about wildlife, this priceless Canadian heritage which we too often take for granted and which needs political support very badly.

subtopic: HISTORIC EVENTS
HISTORIC EVENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise today to recognize Pakistan's National Day. This young nation was proclaimed a republic on this day in 1956. This special day marks the beginning of its nationhood which allowed Pakistan to help to determine the destiny of its people. Pakistan is striving to achieve a better democratic system and an improved standard of living for its people.
Canada is well recognized for the contributions it has made to this country through various CIDA development efforts over
the years in areas such as agriculture, immunization, and transmission of hydroelectricity.
Canada has been made richer by having among its cultural mosaic Canadian citizens of Pakistan origin. I for one would vouch that they have made a tremendous contribution to our country and to Canadian society as a whole.
I am proud to have citizens of all cultural origins in my riding of Etobicoke North. I am pleased to be able today to pay tribute to those of Pakistan origin.

subtopic: SEARCH AND RESCUE
SEARCH AND RESCUE
subsubtopic: DELAY IN RESPONDING TO ACCIDENT ON TRAWLER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the House saw the Minister of Transport's (Mr. Crosbie) cavalier attitude and joking response to an occurrence which could have seen a tanker break in half and result in the worst oil spill in Newfoundland's history. It is clear that this Government is waiting for a disaster to happen. We hope that it will not involve danger to life, because we fear that the search and rescue facilities of the Coast Guard would not be able to respond.
Last Wednesday a crewman aboard the trawler Osprey lost his leg in an accident at sea. Search and rescue at Gander could not help because the only helicopters they have are not equipped with any de-icing capability and could not take off. The trawler took almost eight hours to reach St. John's with the injured crewman and no medical help. This is unacceptable.
On any given day as many as 60 trawlers can be operating off the coast of Newfoundland alone with more than 1,000 crewmen aboard. If the weather is bad they are on their own in case of serious accidents or other marine emergencies.
When will the Government realize that helicopters that cannot fly in bad weather are useless in an emergency?
I call upon the Government, especially the Minister of Transport, to update the search and rescue helicopter fleet and establish a station in St. John's, or at sea on a Coast Guard vessel. Our fishermen, marine workers, and oil workers need more protection than they are getting from the Government.

March 23, 1988

subtopic: HISTORIC EVENTS
HISTORIC EVENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, March 25 marks the one hundred and sixty-seventh anniversary of the independence of modern Greece. It is only fitting that this day be given due recognition because of the importance of Greece and its history and the impact that this has had on western civilization for almost 2,500 years. Much of western culture and western civilization, and the democratic form of government, can trace their roots to Greece, the cradle of democracy.
In spite of the fact that Greece was occupied by numerous successive invaders for some 1,800 years prior to 1821, the Greek culture and Greek traditions, together with the Greek language and religion, were never subdued or diminished, but continued to flourish even under the most difficult, oppressive, and tyrannical overlords that occupied the country.
I would like us as Members of this House and all Canadians to join with my fellow Canadians of Greek descent in celebrating March 25, not only as the National Day of Greece, but as a shining beacon emblematic of all things that have helped to shape a large part of our Canadian way of life.

subtopic: FILM INDUSTRY
FILM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night we witnessed first hand at the Ninth Annual Genie Awards that Canada does have a film industry that can compete with the best in the world. Last year the world was talking about Decline of the American Empire, and this year it is Un Zoo La Nuit which won in all nominated categories. All Canadians will be biting their nails at the Academy Awards with its nomination for an Oscar.
More Canadian films and television programs than ever before were presented at festivals in Canada and around the world, and more were winners, not only in attracting audiences at the box office but also on television screens in every major world market.
Last night was not all celebration. Quebec film maker, Rock Demers, eloquently expressed concerns about the Government's lack of commitment to the arts. He stated that the Government should place more money into the arts, less into nuclear subs, ban its censorship Bill C-54, and forget about free trade.
It took a decade of painstaking public and private action to create the structural impetus for Canadians films and television to flower. Now the Government wants to reverse itself and kick the supports and platform from under this industry. I would strongly suggest that the Government heed this advice from an industry that knows what it is all about.

subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS
PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, next Sunday we celebrate the victory of Mirabel farmers who, twenty years ago, heard on the radio they had just been expropriated to build an airport.
It took these farmers nearly twenty years to have this gross error set right. Unwilling to admit publicly it had made a mistake, the Trudeau Government preferred to harass its victims instead of giving them a fair deal.
When the Conservatives came in with Brian Mulroney, and thanks to the support and sympathy of the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) and the Hon. Member for Argen-teuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault), the situation was finally normalized.
Thanks to the C.I.A.C., the most tenacious citizens' group Quebec has ever known, its members were able to survive, and also thanks to the determination of its first chairman, Mr. Goyer.
Mr. Speaker, Quebecers and Canadians should pay tribute to Mr. Jean-Paul Raymond of Mirabel who continued this struggle for freedom with leadership and perseverance.

subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Premier of Quebec claims to be very concerned about the environment. A non-profit foundation supported by the Premier (Mr. Mulroney) and the federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), is planning a fund-raising campaign for the environment. Should we rejoice? Will Quebec's environment be in good hands?
Unfortunately, the same Ministers are taking action that puts the environment at risk. The free trade agreement will have a disastrous impact on the environment by encouraging the export of non-renewable resources and the use of energy resources that cause pollution. Furthermore, the Government of Quebec is planning more energy mega-projects, despite the fact that these projects are harmful to the environment.
The Ministers supported the Brundtland Report, whose fundamental principle is sustained development. However, decisions taken subsequently by the governments have failed to respect the recommendation that environmental considerations be incorporated in economic decisions. Talking about the environment is useless if our actions do not reflect what we say.
March 23, 1988

POLITICAL PARTIES
subsubtopic: LONG DISTANCE TELEPHONE CHARGES-POSITION OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, formerly the cost of providing telephone service was dependent on the distance between the points served. Modern communications technology is obliterating this dependence. As a result, in relative terms, the cost of long distance service should decline and that of local service should increase.
I am therefore dismayed by the NDP position outlined by the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) last Friday who boasted of his Party's obstruction to rate rebalancing. subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: IRAN-IRAQ WAR-CALL FOR HOSTILITIES TO END
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the war between Iran and Iraq is in its eighth year now. All the world has watched helplessly and with horror as these two countries have wasted and slaughtered their youth, as they have polluted their common marine heritage in the Gulf, and now as they have added a new dimension, not only the war of the cities but the use of chemical weapons.
I would hope that all Members of the House would join with me in saying to both countries that they have no right to pollute the planet in the way they are doing in the Gulf, they have no right to use chemical weapons, they have no right to carry on this madness, and, in the name of all that is holy, they should stop that war now.

March 23, 1988

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am holding a copy of a letter written by Mr. Gordon Sinclair, President of the Air Transport Association of Canada, to the Minister of Transport on February 23, 1988. It is a three-page litany of complaints that Canada's new security systems are not working.
Mr. Sinclair said: "The system is causing delays and major expenses". He went on to say: "We have no control on the system. It is not performing as promised".
In light of Mr. Sinclair's three-page litany of examples why the system is not working, and in light of the shocking spectacle on The Journal last night of employees saying they are not properly trained, is the Minister prepared to accept the unanimous recommendation of the Standing Committee on Transport last October that airport security be taken out of the hands of the airline industry itself, which is in a conflict of interest, and put into the hands of Transport Canada so that adequate standards can be maintained?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: AIR SAFETY
subsubtopic: AIRPORT SECURITY-PRESIDENT OF AIR TRANSPORT ASSOCIATION OF CANADA'S LETTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will ignore the silly adjectives that the Hon. Member used in his question. Of course, he cannot have it both ways and claim that the aviation representatives are complaining about delays, and then say we have an inadequate security system. It must be working if the aviation industry is complaining about delays.
When I have gone through the system, perhaps I look suspicious, but I have always been thoroughly checked. I empty all my pockets and I still buzz. I still have to be searched. Perhaps it is personal magnetism.
Since the Air-India incident of several years ago, we have spent an additional $60 million on improving security systems at our airports. We know that that is not perfect. We know that the system can occasionally be gotten around.
On April 14, 1986, a task force was appointed by my predecessor on this matter. It reported on May 15. The report was approved at the end of May. We have given contracts since for new training programs. We have trained 115 supervisors and trainees at Cornwall with a five-day course.
We now have ready audio-visual material and written manuals. They were ready in English in January and in French in March. We are now ready to ensure that proper training is implemented for all who work in the system.

We have heard from security employees who have gone to work after two and a half hours' training and one with three years' training, that they do not know their jobs. It is not a laughing matter.
I ask the Minister again if he is prepared now in the name of finally doing the proper thing to accept the all-Party unanimous recommendation of the Standing Committee on Transport that security at Canada's airports not be done on the cheap, that it be taken out of the hands of airlines and taken over by Transport Canada, the Government of Canada, to ensure that members of the travelling public can believe the Government when it tells them that the system is secure. subtopic: CANADIAN MULTICULTURALISM ACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, March 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crombie that Bill C-93, an Act for the preservation and enhancement of multiculturalism in Canada, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: CANADIAN MULTICULTURALISM ACT
speechtext: When the House rose yesterday, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) had the floor. Since he is not in the House, I now recognize the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano).

subtopic: CANADIAN MULTICULTURALISM ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this very important debate on Bill C-93, an Act for the preservation and enhancement of multiculturalism in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, Canada has welcomed people from all over the world who come here to find freedom, social peace and economic prosperity. From the first immigrants, whether they were French, Irish or Scottish, down to the recent waves of nationals from Asian countries and including the great migration that took place after the war, when so many immigrants came over from Europe, they have all found in Canada a country that was growing and especially, Mr. Speaker, a country where dreams could become a reality.
Like thousands of people from all parts of the world who became Canadian citizens, my family and I are very grateful to Canada and Canadians for welcoming us as brothers and for giving us a chance to participate fully in the life of our community, our city and our new country.

I feel that the most concrete way in which we can express our gratitude is to pursue an active role in the country we have chosen. We want to continue to progress toward greater harmony and prosperity. Our objective is to create a Canada which reflects the ideals and ambitions of its citizens.

As members of Canada's various cultural communities, each one of us brings with him his own cultural baggage. Each one

March 23, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
of us, Mr. Speaker, brings his traditions and knowledge which have helped to give Canada its unique character and a uniquely dynamic social and economic thrust.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the more our cultural communities are strong, alive and dynamic, the more Quebec and Canada will be strong and productive. This is why a great majority of Canadians support a generous, open and, most important, nondiscriminatory immigration policy.
The family reunification program has always been the favourite of Canadians, we should re-establish this program and make it a cornerstone of our immigration policy. We must improve our system to make it more effective and reduce the frustrations of those who want to sponsor new immigrants. Many people in my riding of Saint-Leonard-Anjou come to see me every week and say that they are willing to provide any guarantee that might be asked of them to have relatives, such as brothers and sisters, come to Canada. Unfortunately, existing legislation and current policies do not allow them to do so.
Mr. Speaker, we have to implement a policy which will allow people to sponsor their relatives and which will promote family reunification to ensure that our country will always remain properous and tolerant. We must also develop a fair and effective system to identify refugees and provide them with adequate facilities on their arrival. Finally, we must eliminate from the system influential but unscrupulous lawyers and advisors who throughout the world mislead thousands of candidates anxious to emigrate to Canada. Those people, who are more motivated by greed than by compassion, cause untold damage to the immigration candidates and to the reputation of Canada.
We must re-establish family class and family unification categories as the unquestionable corner-stone of Canada's immigration policy. We must introduce a more effective and expeditious processing to resolve the lengthy delays and frustration which Canadians encounter in sponsoring immigrants. We must establish and implement a refugee determination system that will provide an efficient and fair processing system. We must address the problem of immigrants who are a part of visible minorities, and especially women who face tremendous and unique challenges. We have to move swiftly and vigorously to eliminate those unscrupulous lawyers and advisors around the world who viciously misinform candidates about our immigration system.

We in Canada already have an advantage in being able to dialogue and deal with the rest of the world in two official languages. When we add to that the linguistic contribution of our cultural communities, we gain access to the richest markets in the world, such as the European Community, Japan, China, and so on. This dialogue between the various
components of our society must be based on mutual knowledge combined with the recognition of our diversity and even sometimes our differences.
Mr. Speaker, pious wishes are all very well, but we have to be realistic and practice what we preach.
As the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) so aptly put it, there are no longer any majorities in this country. One way or another, all Canadians belong to a minority and we are all equal.
Mr. Speaker, here is what former Quebec Minister Paul-Gerin Lajoie had to say about a new immigrant:
If we expect him to like our culture and feel at home in Canada we must not give him the impression that he has to shed his own identity and forget all about his own cultural background. He went on to say unequivocally: "The only way he can make a useful contribution to Canada is to remain faithful to his past. His integration will be all the more real that he be allowed to lead a full life in Canada. It will be worthwhile only to the extent that his fellow citizens benefit from his presence and find enrichment is such diversity."
In fact, the true purpose of multiculturalism is not only to give people a chance to become part of Canadian life, but also to live in Canada and continue to develop their own culture. As Canada and its cultural communities develop their cultural strengths, we will have a strong Canada, a prosperous Canada, a Canada that will be able to compete with the rest of the world.
Once we have perceived and acknowledged this fact, it is much easier to create a cultural dialogue and to acknowledge that we are all genuine parties to this dialogue. To fight racism, to harmonize diversity, to develop a consensus among diverging attitudes, and to make equal opportunity apply to all is no mean challenge, Mr. Speaker, for a country or for a people! A very recent study in the United States found that despite the heroic struggles of black leaders like Martin Luther King, the general perception was that racism continues to exist at a level almost as dramatic as it was during the sixties. The forms it takes may not be as visible as they were when segregation was still legal, but its impact remains practically unchanged, Mr. Speaker. Unfortunately, Canada is not impervious to such attitudes or to their impact.
By the year 2000, three out of five people in Montreal will be of ethnic origin. Today, it is already fifty per cent. This means that Canadians of all origins, especially those who live in big cities, will have to make a quick mental and behavioural adjustment to this situation, and especially to the phenomenon of visible minorities. This takes time and energy, Mr. Speaker, and above all, it requires tolerance.
We need moral and political leadership. Token appointments to second class positions and administrative bandaid solutions are a thing of the past. We must now define new directions, generate innovative ideas and identify today's pressing problems. We have indeed come a long way under previous Liberal governments. Today, however, we must take a hard look at new challenges. We must respond to the new aspirations of our children, of members of our cultural
March 23, 1988

communities who represent a second or third generation. Their attitudes, needs and objectives are not necessarily those of their parents or yours, or mine Mr. Speaker.

The present Government has clearly not understood Canada's multicultural reality of the 1980s, and understands even less the coming reality of the 1990s. Despite the election promises of 1984, the situation has not improved. The lack of government direction has produced nothing but stagnation, confusion and, in my opinion, a deterioration which will, sooner or later, heighten social agitation.

It was just a matter of polishing his campaign image for our cultural communities. Last December, the Government tabled a Bill on multiculturalism, referred to everywhere as being without scope or substance. Instead of giving multiculturalism the kind of support bilingualism is given through the Official Languages Act, the Conservative Government's Bill merely provides a legislative framework for the existing program and extends the principles of multiculturalism to various branches of the Government. In three and a half years, Mr. Speaker, we have had three Ministers of State (Multiculturalism). That is how important this vital issue is to the Government!
Although the operation to launch this Bill was packaged in a glossy brochure, everyone realized the Government was merely making a symbolic gesture that could not hide the lack of substance. Mr. Speaker, throughout the Bill we read constantly: "The Minister may... ", but never a sentence that says: "The Minister shall..." Will our cultural communities always be at the mercy of a change in government or a change of ministers?

The same half-hearted approach was taken by the Government in the area of appointments.
With seemingly impressive numbers, the Government claims to have treated the cultural communities well in this regard. However, looking closely at the appointments, they have been at low levels in Crown corporations, the bureaucracy, and often in strictly advisory organizations.
Canada's cultural communities deserve better. To everyone's benefit, we should be able to find Canadians of ethnic backgrounds involved in all sectors, in decision-making roles at the highest levels of bureaucracy right up to the presidency of any Crown corporation.

So we are still at square one. The Conservative Government cannot be relied on to forge ahead, it has just tabled Bill C-93 last December, and that is as far as it will go. The Bill is a positive proof that it simply cannot see the sociological evolution and respond with fairness and compassion to the needs of Canadians, regardless of their origins.
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, multiculturalism has always been part of the Liberal vision of Canada. Proud of its tradition and many achievements in promoting Canadian multiculturalism, the Liberal Party purposely envisages what Canada might be in the 1990s. Architect of the first and now the second stage of multiculturalism, our Party still maintains a broader long-range perspective whose strength is its very foundation and which is at one with the new generation of Canadians and Quebecers. This leadership reflects our conviction that a policy can never be an end in itself but an ever-fresh challenge which calls for unrelenting efforts and unconditional selflessness.
More than anyone else our Leader of the Opposition is aware of the tangible contribution and vital role of cultural communities in today's and tomorrow's society. What we want is to find dynamic avenues, still more worthwhile programs to be implemented with logic and coherence so as to maximize the scope and impact of all our initiatives in immigration and multiculturalism.

Most of the people came to a new land with an undying promise of hope and purpose. Therefore, we in this House must recognize one inescapable reality, namely, that history has placed you and me, Mr. Speaker, within a common border and under a common law. All of us, from the wealthiest and most powerful of men to the weakest and poorest of children share one precious possession-the name "Canadian".

And so, Mr. Speaker, I want to tell my colleagues in this House that I am proud to be a Canadian. I am proud to belong to a cultural community. I am proud as well to contribute to a political Party which has always been conscious of the multicultural reality and which has never skimped in terms of measures designed to enable our communities to fulfil their aspirations within the great Canadian mosaic.
Mr. Speaker, I feel confident that we can achieve the dialogue of cultures, that we can shape the Canada of the 1990s to reflect its wide variety of citizens. Mr. Speaker, let us give ourselves the tools to build a Canada where we can stand united, and let us give ourselves the tools to build a Canada to our own image.

subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to speak for an undue length of time, but I believe that even a non-controversial Bill on which there is allParty agreement deserves some expanded explanation in order that Members of the House will know what we are doing and those who are observing today's proceedings will understand what Bill C-102 is about. It certainly cannot in any way be described as a major Bill, but it is nonetheless important. It is certainly important to the 2,500 Inuvialuits in the Western Arctic and the Inuvialuit Regional Corporation which represents this group of aboriginal people who live north of 60.
The Bill contains only one clause. That single clause amends the definition of agreement in a previous statute passed by Parliament in June, 1984. That previous statute to which I refer was the Bill that ratified the Inuvialuit final agreement which came out of a very protracted period of negotiations arising out of a claim in the Western Arctic put forward by the Committee on Original Peoples Entitlement, known as COPE. In the past we often spoke about the COPE agreement, the COPE negotiations and so on.
During one part of my parliamentary career it was my privilege-one that I consider to be a very special privilege-to assist in that negotiation process. That assistance in only a small way led to an agreement in principle which was reached prior to the election of 1979. That agreement was reached under the then Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Hon. Hugh Faulkner, who was the Member for Parliament for Peterborough.
When the Clark government took office, this agreement in principle was put on hold in order to pursue and consider certain changes which the Government thought to be necessary. I will not dwell on that unduly, but there were some difficulties to which the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) will probably want to refer if he is speaking on the Bill today.
However, when a new Liberal government took office in 1980 those difficulties were recognized and efforts were renewed to try to achieve a new agreement in principle and a final agreement. That did not happen quickly. While it took some time to achieve this, finally, on March 28, 1984, it was announced by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Hon. John Munro, that a COPE final agreement had been approved by Cabinet.
March 23, 1988

On June 4 it was signed by that Minister and the representatives of COPE. On June 26, the Western Arctic Inuvialuit Claims Settlement Act, Bill C-49, was passed by the House of Commons.
That agreement to which I referred was very large and complicated. Like any agreement that is drawn up in some haste, it had a number of minor difficulties, such as punctuation mistakes, spelling and typing errors and, in one case, an incorrectly drawn map. Like some of the first drafts of essays many of us have written in the past, it needed a lot of work. However, there was so much anxiety to get this agreed to and ratified by Parliament, many of those details were overlooked.
Last year, all of these necessary corrections were quite properly made by Order in Council in what we would call housekeeping changes. A few years prior to that Order in Council, another Order in Council permitted the Petroleum Incentives Program to be applicable to Inuvialuit lands. One can see immediately that that is a dead issue, for all intents and purposes, because since December 3, 1987-the last day to incur any eligible expenses under PIP-and April this year, all eligible claims must be in. To the best of my knowledge, this has no applicability to the Inuvialuit people.
However, I am sure that these two Orders in Council were of some concern to the Government because Orders in Council are always under the watchful eye of the statutory instruments committee. The statutory instruments committee is not at all pleased about changes being made which in fact ought to be properly ratified by Parliament.
Finally, Bill C-102 makes it clear for the future that when non-substantive amendments are agreed to, "consent by Canada" means precisely and exactly consent by Governor in Council. That is how the Statutory Instruments Committee prefers it. It wants parliamentary approval and parliamentary authority for Orders in Council, even if they are routine and housekeeping in nature. If an amendment in the future is nonsubstantive, it will be done by Order in Council.
Of course, if amendments in the future have anything to do with the terms in the agreement that actually affect benefits or any specific aspect of the agreement, then it must come before Parliament for ratification and approval.
Let me describe some of the principles and benefits contained in this agreement. The agreement involves 2,500 Inuvialuit people living in six Arctic settlements: Sachs Harbour, Holman Island, Paulatuk, Tuktoyaktuk, Inuvik, and Aklavik.
There were at least three main objectives that were recognized throughout the negotiating process as essential ingredients of a just and fair settlement. The first was the preservation of Inuvialuit culture and values within a changing northern society. The second was the preparation of the Inuvialuit to be equal and effective participants in the northern and national economies and in society in general.
Western Arctic (Inuvialuit Settlement Act)
The third being the promotion and the preservation of the Arctic's wildlife, biological productivity and natural environment. There are no groups of people in Canada, even the most ardent environmentalists, who have a better philosophical and ancient tradition in respect of preservation of the natural environment than do the Inuvialuit.
What about benefits? The agreement we are talking about intended to protect the rights of the Inuvialuit as Canadian citizens and as aboriginal people under the Constitution Act. It is very important to emphasize over and over again that negotiating these agreements which confer special rights, which I will mention in a moment, in no way cuts off or excludes these people from the normal rights of Canadian citizens. That is why I am such a strong advocate of the recognition of aboriginal rights and the settlement of aboriginal title. Even where it leads to a very high degree of self determination, in no way can it ever be described as some kind of pseudo or semi apartheid. It is because the larger society, the dominant society of which we are a part, in no way excludes access to any of its institutions or to any of its rights. It says that because aboriginal people had established themselves many thousands of years ago-in fact, a recent archaeological estimate is that the origin of these people in North America can be dated back 100,000 years. I am not about to become involved in archaeological disputes about time. I simply accept that aboriginal people were here since time immemorial. We can put whatever figure we want on it.
Aside from conferring or recognizing that they have the rights that all of us enjoy, what are these special rights that go into this agreement because of aboriginal title? Very briefly, they are wildlife harvesting rights, land ownership and management, surface and sub-surface rights and environmental protection; that is, screening and review bodies. Economic and social development is encouraged.
Then, there is the issue of compensation, which includes $152 million through annual payments over 13 years. That calculation, that agreement, is based on dollars at the time. Those dollars are calculated in 1977 terms. That takes into account inflation. The annual payments are to continue until 1997. There is an economic enhancement fund of $10 million, and $7.5 million for social development. Inuvialuit ownership of 91,000 square kilometres of land is recognized. There are surface and sub-surface rights to which I referred earlier of
11,000	square kilometres. There are also certain exclusive and preferential hunting and fishing rights, structures for wildlife management, a conservation regime for the Yukon, northern slope, including a national park west of the Babbage River and a territorial park on Herschel Island.
Those are just some of the items contained in this agreement that was ratified in June of 1984.
In return for the provision of a range of rights, benefits and compensation, what did the Inuvialuit do in exchange for that?

March 23, 1988
Western Arctic (Inuvialuit Settlement Act)
What they did was surrender their interest in and to certain lands in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon and adjacent off-shore islands and waters. In other words, the Government of Canada recognized the existence in this part of Canada of aboriginal title. I refer to the Mackenzie Delta in the western Arctic. The right of Canada, or as we sometimes say the right of the Crown, has been affirmed by way of agreement which flowed from the negotiations and the settlement of a claim.
I cannot end my remarks without repeating once again, and I know I do it perhaps too often but I do so because I feel strongly about it, that it is my view that the Government of Canada still has it all wrong in its understanding of what constitutes aboriginal title. I repeat again categorically and outright that aboriginal title is not merely an awkward, embarrassing and difficult lien, a shadow or an encumbrance on the Crown right. That is what the experts in the Department of Justice would like us to believe. I cannot accept that.
They would argue that despite recognizing aboriginal title in those terms and agreeing to negotiate a settlement, the Crown right is and the Crown right remains at all times and in every instance pre-eminent. I say, not so. I disagree. Aboriginal title precedes the Crown right and where surrender has not occurred then that aboriginal title in my view takes precedence over the Crown right.
How I ask, historically, could suddenly the Crown right take pre-eminence over aboriginal title? How did that happen? It could only have happened on one kind of historical basis that I am able to understand; that is, if one asserts the divine right of monarchs and one says that the God that was believed in by those who came from Europe was a more powerful God. Therefore the power that the Crown had from that God, that right, remains pre-eminent.
All of that theological nonsense has long been thrown in the ash can of history. That is why we have democracies, Sir. Here in Canada we have one vestige of this divine right concept. It is what we use to hammer the aboriginal people over the head with to say, "Well, whatever you do in your negotiations with us do not think you are talking to an equal here. This is not an equal process at the negotiating table. We will give you something. We will toss you some bucks. We will give you some land and we may even let you fool around a little bit with running some of your own affairs. But do not for a moment get up on your high horse and think that your claim is in any way equal to our claim. Our claim, the Crown right, is always and forever pre-eminent".
To that I say nonsense. That point of view is being chipped away at little by little by little. We have on our side a number of important court decisions that have chipped away at it. Eventually, that ridiculous outdated structure of the preeminent Crown right based on the divine right of monarchs will come tumbling down. We in Canada will have to negotiate these outstanding aboriginal claims based on aboriginal title. We are going to have to sit down in a serious way to negotiate as equals.
More about that on another day, because that is a full debate. I wish to end now simply by saying that I have been in contact regarding Bill C-102 with the Inuvialuit Regional Corporation which advised me:
This will confirm for you the substance of our phone call of Friday, December 4, 1987, indicating that the proposed legislation amending the Western Arctic (Inuvialuit) Claims Settlement Act has been discussed with us by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and meets with our approval. Your support for this Bill and efforts to achieve unanimous consent permitting expeditious passage in the House are greatly appreciated.
It is signed by Mr. Roger T. Gruben, Chief Regional Councillor for the Inuvialuit Regional Corporation.

subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too am pleased to participate in today's debate on an Act to amend the Western Arctic (Inuvialuit) Claims Settlement Act. As my friend from Cochrane-Superior has pointed out, the process with which we are dealing today is second reading and third reading debate on Bill C-102. It is timely in that several of the amendments have already passed into history. However, the amendment proposal is important for future business to be consensually and mutually negotiated and agreed upon between the Government of Canada and the Inuvialuit.
I am pleased to also understand that agreements have been reached between the Government of Canada, for example, the Government of the Yukon so that when future proceedings are taking place they are also involved in and informed of the process that is taking place.
My friend has covered some of the points. I think it is important for the record to have a bit more of the history of the original settlement Act, what it means, who was involved and how it came to be.
The Committee for Original People's Entitlement, COPE, as it was widely known in the media and here in the House of Commons and in committees, was the key structure that dealt with the negotiations process in the original agreement that was signed by the then Prime Minister Trudeau and Mr. Munro as the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Simon Reisman was the chief negotiator for Canada, Dennis Patterson was for the Government of the Northwest Territories. He is now the leader of that Government. Chris Pearson represented the Government of the Yukon. He has now gone from politics. For the Committee for Original Peoples' Entitlement at that time it was Peter Green, who was President. He signed together with Charles Haogak, Sam Raddi, Billy Day, Eddie Gruben, Bertha Ruben, Annie Gordon, Elsie Klengenberg, Nellie Cournoyea, Andy Carpenter, Robert Kuptana, Nelson Green, Mark Noksana, Renie Arey, Agnes Semmler, and Bob DeLury, the Chief Negotiator for COPE. At that time it was witnessed by Richard Nerysoo, Maurice Lafontaine, Michael Flavell, and Randal Pokiak.
It was an important moment in time. The Chief Negotiator, Bob DeLury who was living in the area of Burns Lake, was a
March 23, 1988

subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will keep to the Bill a little more than perhaps did the previous speaker. I want to point out that this Bill does three things. It incorporates into law three agreements that have already been made between the Inuvialuit Regional Corporation and the Governor in Council of Canada.
The first one of these deals would be retroactive application of PIP grants on certain Inuvialuit lands. Inuvialuit lands are private lands. They are not public lands anymore. Title to them has been conveyed to the Inuvialuit organizations. We no longer have PIP grants. They went the same way as the rest of the National Energy Program, fortunately, but apparently there must have been applications made for PIP grants for work done on Inuvialuit lands.
When we get to Committee of the Whole perhaps the Minister would be kind enough to explain how this comes about, how much money is involved, how many dollars worth of PIP grants are to be given, if they have not been given already, and to which corporations.
The second thing we do in this Bill is to correct 14 pages in all of errors that appeared in the Inuvialuit final agreement. There are reams and reams of errors that came to light and now have to be corrected. Most of them are of a typographical nature. Quite a few deal with land descriptions, wrong latitudes and longitudes. This came about as a result of the
March 23, 1988

undue haste toward the summer of 1984 by the then Minister, the Hon. John Munro. He knew in the election to be held later that year that he and his Government would stand very little chance of re-election and he wanted to get a feather in his hat. He pushed this matter before he had dotted all the i's and crossed all the t's.
It is also interesting to note that at that time the great Liberal negotiator was none other than our good friend Simon Reisman. In occurs to me that if these 14 pages of errors are a sample of that hon. gentleman's handiwork, I hope he has done a little better with the free trade agreement.

subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I know when we discussed the Inuvialuit Bill way back on June 26, 1984 some of those errors were already apparent, especially those dealing with land descriptions. I pointed them out at that time and I remember questioning the Parliamentary Secretary in Committee of the Whole. He said, "Don't nit-pick. Don't bother with those little errors. They are not important. You should have faith in the negotiators. They have done a good job. It is not for you or I to read through the fine print. We can leave that up to the negotiators and the people in the government departments. What is the difference between 68 degrees and 69 degrees? It doesn't make any difference."
I stand here today and feel somewhat vindicated. I have the pleasure of being able to say, "I told you so". It doesn't do me much good, because it is all water under the bridge now, but it gives you a nice feeling.
The third thing today is to amend the amending formula. Under the old Article 3(13) you need an agreement by Canada and the IRC. Presumably that meant an active Parliament to make any change at all. Now Canada is represented by the Governor in Council and the IRC can be done by the Order in Council route. When you have these very complex lengthy agreements you need some form of flexibility. At the same time, I share some of the concerns mentioned by the previous two speakers.
In the Canadian Constitution, if you look at Sections 25 and 35, Mr. Speaker, you will see that we have constitutionally enshrined, not treaties and land claims settlements but the rights that flow from there. If you want to make a change there, you have to go by the whole amending formula-seven out of ten provinces and 50 per cent of the population. This requirement will shortly need to be changed to unanimity. Then at the other end of scale we are making it extremely easy. All you need is a little Order in Council to make changes. I do not know if we have the balance right. It all depends, I guess, on what you can change by the Order in Council route. Perhaps when the Minister speaks in committee he can explain to us what types of changes will be made under the new Subsection 3(13) and what types of changes cannot be made by that simple route.
Western Arctic (Inuvialuit Settlement Act)
Perhaps you will forgive me, Mr. Speaker, for looking back just a little over what has happened in the last three and one half years or so since the land claims agreement came into effect. I do not want to take up too much of the House's time doing this, nor do I not want to address every issue that I addressed in the lengthy speech I gave on June 26, 1984. At that time I pointed out the bureaucratic nature of the agreement.
It is unfortunate that native organizations negotiating these land-claim agreement so often become the mirror images of the government bureaucracies with which they have to deal. We end up with an extremely complex and bureaucratic settlement which needs continuous administration. I made that point at the time, and that has come to light over the years.
There was a myriad of boards and committees to be established to administer the settlement. Now the Inuvialuit regional corporations and the others that were set up are in the process of trying to amalgamate to become more workable. At that time, one of my main points was the collective rather than the individual nature of the settlement and what that would likely lead to. I think I deserve at least seven out of 10 on my predictions on that score.
What has happened now is that those people who are part of the system, members of the bureaucracy, or those who hold elected positions within the Inuvialuit organizations, seem to be doing okay, but it is debatable whether or not the people who are not part of that system, the ordinary guys on the street, so to speak, are getting a lot of advantage from the settlement. When I talk to people, I find that there are always questions in their minds about where the money goes. We know that there is approximately $170 million involved in this and I get asked questions like why some of that money is down in Bermuda instead of in Inuvik. People question consultant fees and those kinds of things.
Perhaps there is some room for improvement. Perhaps we should learn from the mistakes we are bound to make as we negotiate these settlements. We have the James Bay and the Inuvialuit settlements, and with the ones that come, perhaps we could learn from the mistakes that have been made and try to get a settlement from which everyone can benefit, not just a new class of people that grows up for administrative purposes.
Now I want to make a few points about one of the things that was not addressed four years ago, but which ought to have been addressed, and this is the question of Mr. William Nasogaluak, proprietor of Canadian Reindeer Limited. Perhaps I should explain what went on in the past.
In the 1920s, I believe, the Government of Canada brought reindeer in from Alaska, drove them overland to the area around Tuktoyaktuk and operated the herd as a government herd for quite a few years. Eventually, it was privatized. It was sold to private individuals and with the reindeer went property in the form of grazing rights. Mr. Nasogaluak acquired the

March 23, 1988
Western Arctic (Inuvialuit Settlement Act)
herd and the grazing rights. However, under the Act and under the Inuvialuit final agreement, his property rights, those grazing rights, were expropriated, taken away from him, without any compensation whatsoever. I cannot recall any other instance of a citizen of Canada being treated so badly by his or her Government.
Were the Canadian Bill of Rights to have paramountcy, as the Hon. John Diefenbaker originally had wanted, and were property rights to be included, as they ought to be in our Charter of Rights and Freedoms under the Canadian Constitution, what happened to Mr. Nasogaluak could not have happened or there would have been an automatic recourse at law.
I feel that the Government of Canada has a moral obligation to make sure that Mr. Nasogaluak is treated properly. We recall that Simon Reisman is quoted to have said, when this was brought to his attention, "What's 15,000 reindeer to the Government of Canada?" It is quite a bit to me, and the property rights of one individual Canadian are important to me.
Can you imagine, Sir, what would have happened if the person whose land had been expropriated had not been a reindeer herder from Tuktoyaktuk but a rancher from Alberta, a farmer from Saskatchewan or someone whose apartment house in downtown Toronto had been expropriated without any compensation?
When we were discussing this matter four years ago in Committee of the Whole, I asked Mr. Gingras, the Parliamentary Secretary who was then representing the Government, the following:
May we have the assurance of the Government that it will deal honestly and
faithfully with the owners of the reindeer herd so that those owners do not find
themselves at a loss as a result of the passage of this Bill?
The answer was:
Yes, Mr. Speaker.
That undertaking given by the Liberal Government of the day was a promise broken. Nothing was done.
The current Minister has tried to get Canadian Reindeer Limited and the Inuvialuit together to negotiate an agreement whereby the Inuvialuit would take over the reindeer herd at a reasonable price. There is an agreement by one who acted on behalf of the Government of Canada, Mr. Gunther Abraham-son, as to what the value of that herd was, but the Inuvialuit would never offer anywhere near the figure that was agreed to.
I would like to have seen the Government step in to provide that extra little bit to make it up. We have $170 million being paid out pursuant to the agreement, so what is another couple of million dollars to provide proper compensation? However, that was not happening.
I understand some of the difficulties the Minister has faced. Although there is an undoubted moral obligation on the part of the Government of today, regardless of the fact that the Party in office has changed, I understand that the advice of the
Department of Justice is that outside of a judicial finding which might arrive in the future, there is no legal obligation on the part of the Government to make that compensation at the present time.
What we have done is to force Mr. Nasogaluak to go to the courts to get recompense or fair treatment. Then, of course, if someone were to ask a Minister of the Crown about the matter, he could say that it is before the courts, we cannot do anything. This is something about which I feel extremely strong. I think justice must be done, and I look forward to the opportunity we will have to question the Minister on this issue when, very shortly, we get to the Committee of the Whole proceedings so that he can tell us what he is now doing and what he will continue to do to make sure that justice will be done.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time and, by unanimous consent, the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Paproski in the chair.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first I would like to thank my hon. friend from Western Arctic. He has posed the three questions that need to be answered.
The first aspect is that with PIP gone, as of April, in terms of any claims, what is the history with respect to the Inuvialuit?
The second question deals with what type of changes will go through Order in Council and what type will require legislation. Is there a distinction there?
Finally, there is the matter of the Canadian Reindeer herd. My hon. friend from the Western Arctic said the Liberal promise had been broken. I found that curious because when the Parliamentary Secretary said "Yes", it was June 26, 1984, and a few weeks later there was an election. It is very difficult for a Liberal Government to fulfil a promise when it is not returned to power by the electorate. However, I accept the argument that a commitment is a commitment and I take the view that a commitment is passed on from one administration to the other. It is a moral commitment and I hope the Minister will tell us that he will not fall back on the legalistic point of view, and that the Government will do what is right.
Those are the questions that were on my mind and I thank my hon. friend from the Western Arctic for articulating them so precisely.

speakerposition: Minister of the Western Diversification Office; Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on the Hon. Member's first question, basically the legislation put forward did not allow for
March 23, 1988

PIPs which were obtainable from Crown land to be obtainable from what was now Inuvialuit land. The proposal, and both Members asked about this, retroactively made it legal to have the PIPs which would have applied to Crown land now apply to Inuvialuit land even though PIPs expired as of April. I am attempting to obtain the dollar figures. I have asked my officials to get this information for Members before we adjourn. If I am not able to do that, I will communicate it in writing to Members who have expressed an interest.
On the second question, all amendments would be by Order in Council. However, as the Hon. Member knows, we would not entertain basic changes that would fundamentally alter the agreement signed between Canada and the Inuvialuit.
On the third question, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic, and I have had discussions on this in the past. The history of the Canadian Reindeer herd has been reviewed by this House. Members who are familiar with it understand that in the Inuvialuit settlement agreement about half the grazing area available to Canadian Reindeer had been transferred to Inuvialuit land. Both my predecessor, the Hon. Member for Rosedale, and I have tried to initiate discussions between two private parties to resolve the concern. I met with both the owner of Canadian Reindeer and the Inuvialuit leadership. We put forward the possibility of arbitration. We hoped both parties would agree to accept binding arbitration even though it was not incumbent upon them to do so. As long as the agreement was there, we would bring into play the experts who could assess the value of the herd at the time. That was acceptable to Canadian Reindeer but not to the Inuvialuit.
In the discussions we have had since, I have attempted to fulfil Canada's obligations in other ways. I want to draw the attention of the House to the fact that I found it a bit difficult. The owner of Canadian Reindeer had, as I understand it, an opportunity to make sales. The Government of the Northwest Territories made those sales very difficult by looking at the export permit which the owner had. At the same time, while Canada was not objecting to the sale, Canada did reserve the right to repurchase 3,000 of the herd. I think that was prudent.
Right now, as my colleague from Western Arctic indicated, there are court actions under way. Starting in May, 1987, the Inuvialuit initiated legal proceedings against Canadian Reindeer Limited in the Supreme Court of the Northwest Territories. Canadian Reindeer in turn launched an action against Canada on September 2, 1987. It also filed a third party notice, I gather, in the Supreme Court of the Northwest Territories. That does make enunciation of ways to resolve this dispute a little more difficult, as Hon. Members will understand. I can say only that we have attempted to arbitrate and would be prepared to continue to do so. I believe there is a business opportunity in the Northwest Territories involving Canadian Reindeer Herd Limited and I hope we are able to maintain that business opportunity.
Western Arctic (Inuvialuit Settlement Act)
I am sorry to be taking so long but I find it difficult to explain the discussions between two private parties as they came to pass through the signing of the final agreement.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, returning to the reindeer question, am I to understand that at the present time the Government of Canada is doing nothing to try to resolve this issue?

speakerposition: Minister of the Western Diversification Office; Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with regard to the attempt to have a binding arbitration between the two private parties, the owners of Canadian Reindeer and the Inuvialuit, I made an offer after meeting with both the owner and the Inuvialuit that we would enter into binding arbitration and assist them in that. That offer was accepted by Canadian Reindeer and not found to be acceptable to the Inuvialuit. After that time, in May of 1987, if I am correct, action was initiated in court.
At this time I am prepared to assist in any form of mediation, but I would not become involved in supporting a case or discussions with either party which would involve the actions taken in court until that action is either concluded or withdrawn.

subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, one of the problems is that the value of the herd is likely to be in decline. There is undoubtedly a lot of poaching going on. The owners of the herd are unable to have a proper harvest because they are scared that as soon as they move the abattoir up there and get it hooked up and ready to go and bring in the slaughterhouse workers, an injunction will be slapped on them. There is a big investment involved in starting up and they would lose many tens of thousands of dollars.
Proper management techniques cannot be applied to the herd and revenue cannot be generated from it by way of meat sales and there is therefore no money to reinvest into the herd. Canada is the loser.
This was a great, successful experiment. We ought to have a reindeer industry in Canada. There are other places in the North where it could be applied. Prices are excellent as a result of the unfortunate circumstances in Europe with the Chernobyl disaster. We should be able to capitalize on that but that is not taking place.
I am afraid that if the legal proceedings run their full course by the time a settlement is made by the court there will be nothing left for anyone.
I know that if the Government of Canada really wants to take it upon itself to do something, whether to change the Canadian Constitution or to enter into a free trade agreement with the United States, it can do it. If the will is there the Government of Canada can do virtually anything. Is it not possible to try to open up negotiations again or to have another go around, another shot at it?
So far the tack taken by the Government appears to have been to get the Inuvialuit and Canadian Reindeer together to negotiate some kind of deal between them. However, I do not think there is any moral obligation on the Inuvialuit to do that if they do not want to. It would be nice if they would, but the moral obligation is on the Government of Canada, not on the Inuvialuit. If the Inuvialuit say, "We do not want to play ball", surely the obligation rests on the Government of Canada to address the issue in another way.
Can we not have another go around at this? Can he not appoint someone to look at it again and meet with the people involved to find out what is happening and see whether there is another avenue of approach? Perhaps he can meet again with some of the principals involved.

speakerposition: Minister of the Western Diversification Office; Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, let me answer the last question first. I find it very difficult to enter into negotiations.
I sincerely believe that there must be a willing buyer and willing seller in order to conclude the agreement.
As the Hon. Member knows, an offer was made of $1.2 million. The independent assessment was that the herd was worth over $5 million. I believe my hon. friend is saying that the Government of Canada should enter into it and make up
March 23, 1988

the difference. I understand and appreciate the way in which he expresses his concern.
Since that offer took place I discussed it with both the Inuvialuit and the owner of Canadian Reindeer. That is when I put forward a proposal in a letter to both parties in which I suggested that I would like to see a contract outlining the conditions for the sale and purchase of the Reindeer herd which is mutually acceptable. I went on to say: "This contract could contain certainly a clause whereby the purchase price would be established through a binding arbitration procedure".
When there are two private individuals, one selling and one buying, it is very difficult for the Government of Canada to come into the middle without some recognition that an arbitrator would be required to make a binding decision. It has been further complicated since that time by the court actions taken by both parties.
I can assure my colleague that I have not washed my hands of this, but I do find it very difficult to be involved in it at this time.

subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to return to a point I was raising with the Minister a moment ago. It concerns changes that can be made. As I understand the amending agreement now, it can only be done with mutual consent. Therefore, if the Inuvialuit or the Government has an idea, they must find a mutually agreeable way to word any change. It then gets the imprimatur of Order in Council and becomes added to the agreement.
Clause 3(2) of the agreement states that: "For greater certainty it is the intention of the parties that this agreement be a land claims agreement within the meaning of Section 35(3) of the Constitution Act, 1982".

If one looks at the wording, it is the intention that it be considered as such, but I would like some clarification from the Minister. Is it protected by the Constitution? What is the difference between the Inuvialuit agreement and a treaty like Treaty 8?

subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND

Mr. Chairman, as the Hon. Member knows, the agreement states that it is considered to be under the protection of the Constitution of Canada. That is the way it reads and that is the consideration of the Government of Canada. It is considered to be under the protection of the Constitution of Canada.
Western Arctic (Inuvialuit Settlement Act)
It is a piece of legislation under that clause of the Constitution which was considered by the House to have protection in the Constitution.
I do not want to put words in my colleague's mouth, but I think he was asking if it is recognized as a treaty. It is recognized as having protection under the Constitution of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of the Western Diversification Office; Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few words to say about the Bill. First, I wish to congratulate the Minister for moving so expeditiously on a particular issue that caught the attention of the nation. I think it is fair to say that when Mr. Mclnnis visited Ottawa and his picture was flashed around the country with his baby I realized that underneath the Minister's tough exterior beats a heart that any socialist might be proud to have.
There are those of us who might be so unkind as to suggest that in spite of all the complaints and the recommendations of the Boyer Commission report, equality for all, the standing committee report and the forget commission report, the Government ought to move in the direction of establishing parental care within the Unemployment Insurance Act. For all these last four years nothing could move the Government or the previous Minister, who is now the Minister of Communications, to move in this direction. The Government did not see fit to move.
What adults and politicians were not able to achieve by logic or by consensus a small baby was able to achieve. I think that is appropriate. I wish to congratulate the Minister for having responded in such a human fashion and in such a sensitive fashion to correct this need.
It happened fortuitously that the other aspect of change which is included in the Bill came about at the same time when two women, one in Halifax and one in Vancouver, gave birth prematurely. The babies had to stay in hospital while the
mothers went home. They, of course, went back to work and when the babies came home from the hospital they went down to the UI office to file for their maternity benefits. However, they discovered to their amazement that they could not collect because they were outside the initial benefit period, which is the first 25 weeks of every claim. Thus the Minister was able to tackle two problems at one time.
In Bill C-116 there are two aspects. First, there is the ability of fathers, when the mothers have died or have become disabled to a point where they are incapable of caring for the child, to collect unemployment insurance benefits, provided they have a major attachment to the workforce, that is, they have contributed 20 weeks of insurable earnings.
The second aspect is with regard to the premature child. The mother will now be able to collect benefits provided it is within a 52 week period.
These are both very laudable moves. This Bill will correct those inequities. Unfortunately, it is our view in the New Democratic Party that this Bill does not go far enough. This Party has said to the Government that it ought to establish maternity benefits for which only the mother is eligible. Those maternity benefits ought to amount to 17 weeks. They ought to be only for the mother. They are not to be shared between the mother and the father.
This is very unlike the position taken by the Official Opposition, the Liberal Party. In fact, the Hon. Member for Hamilton East announced that she was entering a Private Member's Bill that would in fact share maternity benefits between the mother and the father. That is totally unacceptable to the New Democratic Party. I am glad to see that the Government accepted that position and refused to have those 17 weeks shared.
We also said that the Government ought to go beyond that and include parental benefits, an additional 26 weeks. All the enlightened countries of Europe have recognized the need for parental benefits within their unemployment insurance programs. We have urged the Government to do this. Not only have we urged it, but so has the Boyer Commission in its report and the parliamentary committee on day care. We are still pushing for it.
We have to accept and take what is being offered because it corrects an injustice. However, we fully recognize that the Minister has established a principle which it will take a New Democratic Party Government to complete. I wish to say to all parents who are watching this debate that that is the only guarantee they have that we will move toward treating parents and children with some justice under the unemployment insurance program.
I wish to say, Mr. Chairman, that we will support this. My leader and gave our commitment in the House that we will expedite this Bill and move it through.
March 23, 1988

I think that this is only fair and just since she participated in the parliamentary day care committee which filed its report in 1987. It had a lot to do with child care and parental care in the unemployment insurance program.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and deal with Bill C-116, a major peace of legislation the purpose of which is to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.
As my NPD friend just did, I want to congratulate the Minister for having responded. Unfortunately, I have also cause for complaints. In this particular matter as in many others, this Tory Government had to wait for a disaster before taking action.
The Minister certainly remember the Forget Commission which cost Canadian taxpayers $6 million. There was also a Committee of the House where all Members were unanimously asking, on the paternity leave issue, a certain equality as far as unemployment insurance benefits are concerned. The House will remember that the Minister tore up this document and threw it into the waste basket, thereby squandering a lot of taxpayers' money. The Government had to wait for a mother to die to take action.
If, at the time, in view of the unanimous recommendations of the House Committee-my friend the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) was quite active on this committee-on the changes to be made to the unemployment insurance legislation to improve the effectiveness of the administration and do justice to people .. .
And while the debate continues with respect to sharing, or the allowances for maternity or paternity leave, to carry forward the weeks eligible for unemployment insurance benefits, we also remember that today still in other instances there is discrimination against older workers.
The Minister has reacted and we commend him for that, but I would be remiss if I failed to congratulate my colleague from Hamilton who put a lot of pressure on the Minister. Otherwise we might not have this Bill. Pressure came from the public, from my colleague from Hamilton, from my colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East, and at long last the Minister came up with Bill C-116 to correct his mistakes, particularly his failure to give serious consideration to the unanimous parliamentary report urging him to change some of the unemployment insurance rules.
Mr. Speaker, indeed we can be positive, but unfortunately I would like the Minister to tell us why every time this Government ... We remember the de-indexation of old age pensions. There again people had to demonstrate, elderly Canadians had to walk on Parliament Hill, Mrs. Denis had to throw insults or
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
show the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) the truth before he would even admit he was wrong. It was the same for the tax on pharmaceutical products, Mr. Chairman. Once more, the Government waited until there had been pressures and a demonstration before deciding to withdraw its proposal. The same happened in the case of unemployment insurance. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) went through a similar experience recently. No one in this Government, in the party opposite, seems able to realize that certain members of our society have needs which differ from those of the majority, of those who are able to make arrangements and pay their own way.
I must congratulate the Minister for having introduced this Bill, but as I said earlier, it is thanks to my colleague for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), my colleague for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), and the entire Liberal caucus, and to the pressures exerted by the population that this Government acted quickly in this instance.
On the other hand, we have to wonder why, since the Minister is making two changes in this Bill, he did not take this opportunity to make other changes as concerns unemployment insurance benefits for older workers who lose their jobs. As he was correcting one injustice and trying to improve the situation, why should we have to wait until there have been more pressures and more representations to have another Bill which will bring about a complete reform of the Unemployment Insurance Plan to provide better equity and more justice for our young poeple? The public, the unions, as well as the employers all requested a complete reform of the Unemployment Insurance Plan, but the Government is making piecemeal changes. This means that all that we are doing now is to correct past mistakes. Such has been the case for the refunds to the 46,000 senior citizens, and thanks again to the early retirees who pressured the Government, they got a grandfa-therly refund.
We have another example now with paternity leave. But speaking of paternity leave, we should ensure that what the minister will be offering tomorrow is not something else than the choice for the family. When the parent at home, either the mother or father, has to look after a child, he or she will be eligible for UI benefits. Under the Bill now before us, only in case of death would the father have automatic eligibility to UI benefits. It is not an opening to sex equality in the sense of choosing, or allowing those people the right of choice.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we in the Liberal Party are proud that this legislation was tabled. We will co-operate as my colleagues did to its speedy adoption. But there are still questions, interrogation marks. It is my hope the Minister will tell us in the first place why he waited for so long. Why did he not anticipate? I would think that governing is not simply correcting, but anticipating the future, rather than simply putting out fires, because on that matter the Minister has been acting like a fireman who puts out fire. Firemen we have no

Elopefully the Minister will indicate and explain why, in the wake of the recommendations made not only by the Forget Commission but the recommendations indeed of the Standing Committee on which three Conservative Members were very active ... The Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) worked on that issue, and I know he is a close friend of the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Hon. Member for Hochelaga-Maison-neuve (Mr. Desrosiers). The support for a greater extension of paternity and maternity leave is unanimous.
Mr. Chairman, it seems there are friendships I was not aware of. But I remember, and I am sure my colleague from the New Democratic Party can testify to that, that the Hon. One must listen, reflect, follow one's heart and then act. If the Minister had done all that immediately, following the recommendations made in the Committee's report, he would have made changes and introduced amendments, and then this particular case would not have become a public issue, the Minister having made provision for such an eventuality at the time.
Incidentally, I wish the Minister would tell us why he waited so long to do something about this case. I also wish the Minister would tell us why ... well, I imagine there are a lot of older workers, all the people from Vickers and Coleco, all those people across Canada, people from the Quebec City area and Sorel who are going to be laid off because of the Conservative Government's decision, and who when they turn 55 go to the Unemployment Insurance office. So he says: I came to get my unemployment insurance cheque. So then the UIC man says: Sure, you paid your contributions, you made sacrifices for so many years, and you and your employer both paid into your pension, because the Government said to be prepared. But unfortunately, we have this Bouchard Bill and now you aren't entitled to full unemployment insurance benefits. Even if you did lose your job. Sure, but I didn't want to lose my job. And the man says: Sure, I realize that, but I'm afraid the Conservative Members and the Minister didn't understand. So I wish the Minister would tell me . . .
I know there are some Conservative Members, maybe not the Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais), since he may have trouble talking to the Minister, but maybe another Member told the Minister that older workers who are losing their jobs wished the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte Marie had something to congratulate the Minister about in this Bill. I wish I could have said thank you to the Minister
today. I wish I could have said congratulations, you were generous! You removed the injustice about paternity leave and extensions and made maternity leave more flexible. But what the Minister should do as well is remove the discrimination against benefits for older workers.
My second question, Mr. chairman-and I would like the Minister to give us a clear and specific answer so I will repeat the question: Why did he waste all that money on inquiries and studies? Why didn't he think of it beforehand? Why didn't he plan ahead so as to bring forward a Bill in time instead of going uphill all the way and always having to react to events and put off fires? Why didn't he take this opportunity to bring forward amendments relating to the pre-retirement of older workers who lose their jobs? He could also have proposed changes to improve eligibility requirements for maternity leave and accessibility criteria for part-time workers.
There were several aspects to the matter. The Minister could have taken that opportunity to correct these mistakes. Of course, the Minister would prefer congratulations. Unfortunately, we cannot congratulate him as much as he would have wanted because had he listened not only to Opposition members but to Government members, he would not have had to flip-flop and be embarrassed the way he is.
Today, the Minister may feel well. But once more I have to ask him to listen to his own heart. Mr. Minister, you sure feel all right. I feel all right too. I had a pension plan in my previous job. With a pension and a Minister's or an M.P.'s salary, you've got to feel all right. But there are thousands of working men and women out there who do not feel that good.
At the end of the month they have to pay for groceries and rent, so when there is no unemployment cheque and they can see the neighbour who used to be a school principal, who had a lot of money to invest in an RRSP, who now gets his money back and enjoys the good life... So it is not a question of whether we parliamentarians feel fine, but whether we have done our job to make sure that the people we represent are feeling fine. I must tell the Minister that I am familiar with his beautiful riding, the beautiful region of Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean-I am their spokesman in the Liberal Party-where I met people who are not at all satisfied with the Minister, even in the riding of Roberval. Older workers in that region are not pleased with the Minister because he does not listen to them, he does not understand them. I also visited the Eastern Townships, and the situation is the same. Older workers, both men and women-and even those of Trois-Rivieres-are reorganizing in Quebec City, and even in Abitibi people are disappointed because they have the impression that their Members of Parliament fail to represent them properly.
Perhaps Hon. Members are saying something because the Hon. Member for La Prairie, I know, had warned him, but my impression is that the Minister should listen a little more and respond with his heart, just as he did yesterday on the immigration issue.

There are three question marks, Mr. Speaker. I still have some time left and I see that the Minister is interested in what I am saying. He is starting to listen. We can feel his heart is opening. Perhaps he is going to tell us, and it is a pity that the Hon. Member for La Prairie is not here ... The Minister may let his heart speak out.
