But you are all here as elected Members of this House, and this is something that affects each and every one of your ridings. We are here to tell civil servants what to do. You operate the way the people who elected us want you to operate.
I am sure that if each ... If there were no TV cameras, I am sure that the Tory Members would tell the Minister that Canadians want him to remove all discrimination against older people. I am convinced that within the Tory caucus, there is not a single Member-except perhaps one or two, because you will find all sorts in that party-who would stand up and suggest that the Government should fall hard on older people.

Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie and the other Members who sat on the House Committee which dealt with the unemployment insurance situation were right to warn us about paternity and maternity leaves.

by the NDP, because whatever our party, we all want what is best for Canadians. I now see that my time has expired, Mr. Chairman. -congratulate him on having included more comprehensive coverage under the Unemployment Insurance Act for maternity and parental leave. I must say that I am very sorry that the federal Government's strategy for child care neglects this very important aspect of child development which is that working parents, either fathers or mothers, must have the opportunity to be at home with their children during the first year of their children's lives.
I think it is very interesting that this case was started by a father. I think it is very natural that the men in this House, some of whom have spoken today, immediately identified with that father who did indeed face a serious situation in being widowed and left with the care of a new infant without the benefit of unemployment insurance.
I would like to remind the men who did identify very strongly with Mr. Mclnnis, however, that there are thousands and thousands of single-women parents who are on welfare and are not eligible for unemployment insurance. We all felt very strongly for Mr. Mclnnis, but let us not forget those thousands of women who are trying to bring up children and new babies and have no choice but to live on very low rates of welfare.

March 23, 1988
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
I would like to congratulate both Mr. Mclnnis and the women who were the guinea pigs whose cases resulted in changes to the Act. I am referring particularly to the case of Cathy MacLean from Nova Scotia, a case I raised in the House when I asked the Minister to use his discretionary powers to assist her. I am glad he did not have to use those powers. Instead, he amended the Act. This also means that Melanie Williams of Vancouver, whose case was raised several times by the Hon. Member for Capilano along with many other women who have had premature babies, will benefit.
Now the mothers of premature babies, babies who have to be left in hospital for a much longer period than normal and need their mothers' care when they come out of hospital, will benefit from the flexibility in the Act that will allow unemployment insurance benefits to be delayed until they are needed. That is a very good move.
These two amendments have significant implications suggesting that the Government is finally accepting the need to incorporate child care provisions in the Unemployment Insurance Act. We are pleased about that. We are also very pleased that these provisions are incorporated under the adoption section of the Act rather than the maternity benefits section of the Act. Maternity benefits that are intended for mothers during the period of time after birth will be protected.
I would join with my colleague in saying that I am very surprised and disappointed that the Liberals, and particularly the Hon. Member for Hamilton East, have not seen the point. They have not been sensitive to the needs of mothers who have given birth and need the protection of maternity leave for their own recovery as well as for the care of their newborns. These mothers must have that right protected under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Incidentally, they should not have to wait for two weeks to apply for unemployment insurance, it should be a 17-week provision. That was the recommendation of the special committee majority report as well.
I will try to cut my remarks short, but I did want to comment on the need for extended and enriched maternity and parental benefits. The Minister knows full well that the Canadian Human Rights Commission, the parliamentary committee on equality rights, the Forget Commission, the New Democratic Party report on child care, as well as many groups across Canada have advocated the doing away with the two-week waiting period and the use of a two-tiered system of maternity and parental leave. Maternity benefits should go to the biological mother and parental benefits to either mothers or fathers. We hope more fathers will take advantage of this. This provision should apply after the first 17 weeks and it should be available for natural as well as adoptive parents.
With so many parents working, it is extremely important that we recognize, as most western European countries have, that parental and maternity leave are absolutely essential. We will make children as well as families suffer if there is no
option for the mother and later the father to be at home during that important first year of a child's life. That should be part of the government child care program as well as part of the programs under the Minister's responsibility.
Let us take a quick look at the provisions in a couple of European countries. France offers 16 weeks for mothers at full pay and six months at up to 100 per cent of maximum earnings for the third or subsequent child. As well, France offers unpaid parental leave of up to two years for both mothers and fathers. Sweden provides 40 weeks for mothers or fathers at full pay and an additional unpaid leave is available when the child reaches the age of 18 months.
Canada ranks 22 out of 23 in all the world's industrialized countries when it comes to the level of benefits paid to women workers who take leave on the birth of children and to fathers. We recommend that there be maternity leave for the first 17 weeks, followed by parental leave, which would allow either parent to have UI coverage. We would like to see this phased in gradually and eventually reach a total of 43 weeks. That is not out of line considering what has been done for many years in European countries.
We also recommend that benefits should be gradually enriched so that low-income parents have a choice. Otherwise, they will be forced to go back to work because they will simply not be able to survive on the low payments.
We were disappointed that the government strategy on child care did nothing to improve maternity and parental leave. It was not even included, and that was a great omission. We believe that this is a very important part of a parental leave program. Therefore, as a New Democrat, I must express disappointment that the Bill did not move beyond establishing the principle of a two-tier benefit system as it should have done by providing comprehensive maternity and parental leave.
We support the Bill for the specific inequities it addresses, but we desperately need a more comprehensive parental and maternity leave program.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleagues for the opportunity to say a few words on the action being taken this afternoon.

March 23, 1988
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
I want to congratulate the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) on the action he has taken to extend unemployment insurance benefits to biological fathers in cases where, because of the death of the mother, the father leaves work to become the primary caregiver of the child, or in the case of a mother who becomes incapacitated to the extent that she cannot care for the child.
The Unemployment Insurance Act is also being amended to make the time limits more flexible where a premature newborn is hospitalized.
The Canadian Human Rights Commission, the Forget Commission, the parliamentary committee on employment, and the Equality for All report all support the concept of extending this type of maternity benefit to fathers.
These changes, as they apply to fathers, were sparked by John Mclnnis, a constituent of mine from Kitchener, Ontario. The mother of this infant girl died from a brain tumour shortly after the birth. Mr. Mclnnis left his work to take care of the baby and when he discovered that maternity benefits were unavailable to him, he turned to living on welfare.
Mr. Mclnnis and I requested a meeting with the Minister to see if there could be some redress for his unique circumstances. Because of the Minister's compassion, we had this meeting, quick action was promised to remedy the situation, and thus we have before us today the present amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
In addition, another amendment that we will be approving today will allow the payment of maternity benefits during a period of up to 17 weeks from the time the baby comes home from the hospital, rather than from the expected or actual date of birth. That will benefit another of my constituents, Sharon Beaucage. This will allow mothers separated from their premature child due to the baby's hospitalization to take their maternity benefits when the baby comes home from the hospital.
I want to commend the Minister and the Government, under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), for acting in the spirit of the following words spoken by a former leader of the Conservative Party, the Hon. Robert Stanfield:
I pledge to you a government prepared to act, impatient with the notion that problems cannot be solved.
I pledge to you a government that will deal openly and honestly with the people and with Parliament, one whose word can be trusted, one of compassion, conscience, commitment and principle.
I commend the Minister of Employment and Immigration. He has proven that governments do indeed listen, can act with reasonable speed, can act with flexibility where required, and with the compassion spoken of by the Hon. Robert Stanfield.
